design_problem.problem_statement: An Amazon Robotics AMR (differential drive, 0.5 m wheelbase) is commanded to execute a precise pick-and-place mission: travel exactly 2.0 m forward along aisle A7, turn exactly 90° right, then stop at shelf slot B3. After executing the command sequence, telemetry shows the robot stopped 18 cm past the target slot and 12° misaligned. The warehouse management system flags a collision risk. Diagnose the failure and redesign the motion model.
design_problem.real_world_context: Amazon Robotics warehouse automation — Proteus and Hercules AMR fleet. Positional accuracy of ±5 cm is required for shelf slot picking. Systematic position error causes downstream logistic failures.

failure_modes.naive_approach: Describe the robot's position as a single distance from the start point along the intended path. Command '2 m forward + 90° turn' is just two numbers: Δd = 2.0 m, Δθ = 90°.
critical_questions: If the robot turns by 45° during what was supposed to be straight motion, where is it now?
How do we describe 'position' when the robot is not pointing in the direction we expect?
What is the minimum set of numbers needed to know exactly where the robot is in the warehouse?
failure_modes.why_it_fails: A single scalar distance cannot represent a 2D pose. The robot's state requires a coordinate frame: position (x, y) plus orientation (θ). Without a rigorous frame definition (world frame, body frame, sensor frames), position commands are ambiguous — '2 m forward' means different things depending on which direction 'forward' is currently pointing.
failure_modes.failure_consequence: The motion command is interpreted in the wrong reference frame. The robot executes '2 m along world X-axis' instead of '2 m along body heading', ending up in the wrong aisle entirely.
failure_modes.scientific_principle: Homogeneous transformation matrices T ∈ SE(2) encode a rigid body's pose as a combined rotation R ∈ SO(2) and translation t ∈ ℝ². Frame transformations chain: T_world_sensor = T_world_body × T_body_sensor. All robot motion commands and sensor readings must be expressed in a consistent, explicitly defined frame.

citation.location: Chapter 3: Rigid-Body Motions, Section 3.1–3.3, Pages 63–100 — SE(2), homogeneous coordinates, frame transforms

failure_modes.naive_approach: Command the robot by setting left wheel speed = right wheel speed = v. For a turn, set one wheel to v and the other to 0. Just scale the speeds intuitively.
critical_questions: Given left wheel speed ω_L = 3 rad/s and right wheel speed ω_R = 4 rad/s and wheel radius r = 0.033 m, what is the robot's linear velocity and angular velocity?
What path does the robot actually trace in the world frame?
How far apart must the wheels be to achieve a 90° turn in exactly 0.5 m of travel?
failure_modes.why_it_fails: Intuitive speed scaling gives no mathematical relationship between wheel velocities and robot pose change. Without the kinematic model, there is no way to compute wheel commands that achieve a desired (x, y, θ) trajectory. The forward kinematics and inverse kinematics of the differential drive must be derived from geometry.
failure_modes.failure_consequence: Wheel speed ratios are chosen by trial-and-error. The robot turns 73° instead of 90° because the wheelbase was not accounted for in the turn calculation.
failure_modes.scientific_principle:
For a differential drive robot with wheel radius r and wheelbase l:
  v = r(ω_R + ω_L)/2  [linear velocity]
  ω = r(ω_R - ω_L)/l  [angular velocity]
Forward kinematics: (ẋ, ẏ, θ̇) = f(ω_L, ω_R, θ). Inverse: given desired (v, ω), compute (ω_L, ω_R). This is the fundamental motion model for all subsequent localization and control.

citation.location: Chapter 3: Mobile Robot Kinematics, Section 3.2.1, Pages 55–68 — Differential drive forward and inverse kinematics

failure_modes.naive_approach: Try to command the robot to move diagonally (e.g., 45° heading change while simultaneously translating sideways) to correct a small lateral position error — treat it like commanding a holonomic drone.
critical_questions: Can a differential drive robot move sideways?
How many velocity commands does a differential drive robot accept?
Why can the robot reach any (x, y, θ) configuration in the plane despite not being able to move sideways instantaneously?
failure_modes.why_it_fails: The differential drive robot has a non-holonomic constraint: its velocity must always be in the direction it is currently facing. The robot cannot move sideways — the constraint equation ẋ sinθ − ẏ cosθ = 0 must hold at all times. Attempting to send a sideways velocity command violates the constraint and is physically impossible.
failure_modes.failure_consequence: The lateral correction command is physically impossible to execute. The robot's wheels skid, IMU detects unexpected acceleration, and the safety monitor triggers an emergency stop.
failure_modes.scientific_principle: A non-holonomic constraint is a velocity constraint that cannot be integrated into a position constraint: Pfaffian form A(q)q̇ = 0. For differential drive: the no-slip condition ẋ sinθ − ẏ cosθ = 0. Despite 2 controllable DOF, the robot can still reach any (x, y, θ) configuration via a sequence of feasible motions — this is small-time local controllability (Chow's theorem).

citation.location: Chapter 1: Introduction to Nonholonomic Mechanics, Section 1.2, Pages 1–20 — Pfaffian constraints, controllability

failure_modes.naive_approach: For faster warehouse navigation, replace the differential drive robot with a car-like Ackermann robot — it goes faster in straight lines.
critical_questions: What is the minimum turning radius of an Ackermann robot?
Can it reverse into a tight shelf slot like a forklift?
What additional constraint does the Ackermann geometry introduce?
failure_modes.why_it_fails: Ackermann steering geometry has a minimum turning radius r_min = l/tan(δ_max) determined by the wheelbase l and maximum steering angle δ_max. In tight warehouse aisles (1.5–2 m wide), this minimum radius may be larger than the available space. The robot physically cannot make the required turn.
failure_modes.failure_consequence: The robot cannot navigate 90° turns in standard warehouse aisles without a multi-point turn, which blocks the aisle for other robots and causes a traffic deadlock.
failure_modes.scientific_principle: Ackermann geometry ensures all four wheels roll without slip during a turn by constraining inner/outer wheel steer angles: cot(δ_o) − cot(δ_i) = l_w/l where l_w is track width and l is wheelbase. The bicycle model simplifies this to a single equivalent front wheel. Turning radius R = l/tan(δ). Critical for path planning: all paths must respect this geometric constraint.

citation.location: Chapter 11: Mobile Robots, Section 11.2.2, Pages 469–474 — Ackermann steering, bicycle model

failure_modes.naive_approach: For maximum flexibility, use 4 mecanum (Swedish) wheels — the robot can then move in any direction at any time.
critical_questions: What is the kinematic model for 4 mecanum wheels at 45°?
What happens to the wheel forces if the floor has a small bump?
Why do omni-wheel robots require a flat, clean floor?
failure_modes.why_it_fails: Omnidirectional robots achieve holonomic motion through passive rollers on mecanum wheels, but the kinematic model requires all 4 wheels to maintain ground contact simultaneously. On uneven warehouse floors, one wheel lifts and the model becomes invalid — the robot drifts unpredictably. Additionally, omni-wheels have higher rolling resistance and are noisier than standard wheels.
failure_modes.failure_consequence: On the slightly uneven concrete warehouse floor, the robot drifts 8 cm per meter of travel. After 20 m, it is in a completely wrong aisle.
failure_modes.scientific_principle:
For a 4-mecanum-wheel robot (wheel angle α = 45°, radius r, platform radius l):
  [v_x, v_y, ω]^T = (r/4) × J × [ω₁, ω₂, ω₃, ω₄]^T
The Jacobian J relates body velocities to wheel speeds. The model assumes no slip at each roller contact point — an assumption that fails on uneven terrain. Selection criterion: use omni-drive only on clean, flat floors when omnidirectional agility is required.

citation.location: Chapter 3: Mobile Robot Kinematics, Section 3.2.3, Pages 73–80 — Omnidirectional wheel kinematics

failure_modes.naive_approach: After selecting differential drive, plan paths as straight-line segments. The robot turns in place at each waypoint, then drives straight to the next one.
critical_questions: What is the robot's effective workspace — can it reach all shelf slots in the warehouse?
How does the non-holonomic constraint affect path planning in tight spaces?
What is the difference between the robot's configuration space and its workspace?
failure_modes.why_it_fails: The robot's reachable workspace is the full 2D floor plane (any x, y reachable), but its maneuverability in tight spaces is limited by the non-holonomic constraint. Some configurations require multi-move sequences. Without analyzing maneuverability, path planners may generate geometrically valid but kinematically infeasible paths.
failure_modes.failure_consequence: The path planner generates a direct path to slot B3 that requires a 180° turn in 0.3 m of space. The robot cannot execute this and halts, blocking the aisle.
failure_modes.resolving_concept_name_ar: قابلية المناورة ومساحة العمل للروبوت المتنقل
failure_modes.scientific_principle: Maneuverability is characterized by two sub-metrics: (1) mobility δ_m — how many instantaneously achievable velocity directions exist; (2) steerability δ_s — how many steerable wheels exist. Total maneuverability μ = δ_m + δ_s. For differential drive: μ = 2 (high maneuverability). The workspace analysis must account for non-holonomic constraints when planning in tight environments.

citation.location: Chapter 3: Mobile Robot Kinematics, Section 3.3, Pages 81–90 — Maneuverability analysis

failure_modes.naive_approach: Command the wheels to spin the right amount and trust that the robot ends up at the target. No position feedback — it's just geometry.
critical_questions: After 10 m of travel, where is the robot really?
How do small errors in wheel encoder ticks accumulate over distance?
What is the mathematical model for position error growth?
failure_modes.why_it_fails: Open-loop control ignores cumulative integration errors. Wheel encoder tick counts are converted to distance via r = wheel radius — but encoder resolution, gear backlash, and slight wheel diameter variations cause small per-tick errors that integrate unboundedly over distance. After 2 m, a 1% wheel radius error produces 2 cm position error. After 50 m, it is 50 cm.
failure_modes.failure_consequence: After a 50-waypoint pick-and-place cycle, the robot is 80 cm from where it thinks it is. It attempts to pick from shelf B3 but reaches into B5, knocking product off the shelf.
failure_modes.scientific_principle:
Dead reckoning integrates the kinematic model over time:
  x(t+Δt) = x(t) + v·cos(θ)·Δt
  y(t+Δt) = y(t) + v·sin(θ)·Δt
  θ(t+Δt) = θ(t) + ω·Δt
Errors are unbounded without external correction. Error covariance grows as Σ_k = F·Σ_{k-1}·F^T + Q where F is the Jacobian and Q is process noise. Odometry alone is necessary but not sufficient — it must be fused with exteroceptive sensing (LIDAR, cameras) for bounded error.

citation.location: Chapter 5: Dead Reckoning Navigation, Section 5.1–5.3, Pages 191–230 — Odometry model, error accumulation, covariance propagation

failure_modes.naive_approach: After adding sensor fusion to correct odometry, assume that wheel encoder ticks always accurately measure ground contact distance — slip is just a minor noise term.
critical_questions: What happens to odometry when one wheel spins on a wet spot?
How does the encoder reading differ from actual ground displacement during slip?
What force must be transmitted to prevent slip?
failure_modes.why_it_fails: Wheel slip breaks the fundamental assumption of odometry: that encoder rotation corresponds directly to ground displacement. When the friction force required to accelerate the robot exceeds μ×N (coefficient of friction × normal force), the wheel slips. During slip, encoder ticks increase but the robot does not move — the odometry model overestimates traveled distance.
failure_modes.failure_consequence: The robot accelerates across a wet patch at aisle crossing. Right wheel slips. Odometry registers 0.3 m travel but actual displacement is 0.05 m. Robot believes it is 0.25 m ahead of its actual position. The corrected position is now too far from the LIDAR map — the localization filter diverges.
failure_modes.scientific_principle: Slip ratio λ = (v_wheel − v_ground)/max(v_wheel, v_ground). Traction force F_traction ≤ μ_s × N. Slip detection: compare IMU acceleration to expected acceleration from wheel speeds. Slip mitigation: traction control reduces wheel torque to keep λ < λ_threshold. Odometry correction: use IMU as ground truth during detected slip events.

citation.location: Chapter 6: Traction and Slip, Section 6.1–6.2, Pages 231–262 — Slip models, traction control, IMU-assisted odometry
